title.narrative: Economic Opportunities for the Poor (EOP) - Sri Lanka

description.narrative: The Economic Opportunities for the Poor (EOP) Program in Sri Lanka aims to stimulate inclusive, private sector-led economic growth and poverty reduction. The overall goal of EOP is to stimulate economic growth that benefits the prospective participants through the engagement with the private sector. The portfolio focuses on high potential industries, economic sectors that have a strong potential both to grow over the medium term and to include and benefit poor and disadvantaged groups in their economic roles as producers, workers, entrepreneurs and consumers. Three main projects under EOP were: the Market Development Facility (MDF); Skills for Inclusive Economic Growth (S4IG); and Local Empowerment through Economic Development (LEED). Of these three projects, only MDF is currently active, while the others have been completed.

description.narrative: Australia supported the ILO's Local Empowerment through Economic Development program (LEEDS+)to establish new supply chains in aquaculture in the former conflict zones of Northern Sri Lanka. A private sea cucumber hatchery was established in 2023 and fisherfolk in target areas were trained in new cultivating techniques. 50% of the farmers in target areas have now adopted these cultivation practises into their farming techniques.

Australian funded MDF program and Ellawala Horticulture, a private agriculture company; commercial cultivation of mango using new technology, collaborated to expand an organic backyard farming model and provided farmers with advisory support. The pilot supported 100 participants harvesting crops and selling surplus produce. Ellawala addressed negative perceptions by emphasising subsistence and clean eating and educating farmers to reconsider agrochemical use. The focus shifted to selling excess produce, leading farmers to recognise the commercial benefits of organic farming. The intervention greatly improved access to safe, nutritious food for communities. Collaboration between MDF and Ellawala positively impacted local agriculture and sustainable practices.

title.narrative: Economic policy reform and management and private sector development

description.narrative: Decades of reliance on single-nutrient fertilisers like urea have degraded Sri Lanka’s soil health and reduced rice productivity, threatening farmer incomes and national food security. Improved fertilisers—slow-release, bio-fertilisers, and crop-specific blends—offer a sustainable solution by enhancing nutrient uptake and restoring soil health. ‍ To support adoption, the Market Development Facility (MDF), funded by the Australian Government’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT), improved distribution and marketing in Ampara, a major rice-growing district in Sri Lanka. During the 2023/24 Maha season, farmers reported stronger roots, fewer empty shells, and healthier soils. ‍ By end-2024, MDF partners sold nearly 10,000 bags of improved fertiliser, generating USD 137,600 (AUD 212,635) in revenue. Over 2,200 farmers collectively earned USD 485,700 (AUD 750,000) in additional income. Yields rose 11%, adding 1,000 tonnes of rice to local supply. While chemical fertiliser use remains unchanged, many farmers are open to reducing usage—supporting long-term food security and climate resilience.

Delivering timely, crop-specific advice on managing pests and plant diseases is vital to safeguarding yields and improving agricultural productivity. Through the Australian-funded Market Development Facility (MDF), the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) expanded a private sector-led digital advisory service, Dialog’s Govi Mithuru, to support climate change adaptation in Sri Lanka’s agriculture sector. The platform provides real-time, localised agricultural advice—including pest alerts—to over 130,000 farmers. This timely information enables early detection and response to pest outbreaks, which are increasing in frequency and severity due to climate change. ‍ In 2024, over 17,700 farmers using Govi Mithuru reduced pest-related harvest losses by at least 60% and the program as a whole cumulatively added an estimated AUD 10.6 million (USD 7 million) in farm income. The service builds resilience by offering scalable, low-cost digital extension support, reducing reliance on overstretched public services, and helping farmers adapt to climate-induced risks. ‍ This investment highlights how digital tools can cost-effectively strengthen disaster resilience and adaptive capacity in vulnerable rural communities, directly supporting DFAT’s climate and food security objectives.

title.narrative: Economic policy reform and management and private sector development

description.narrative: In 2022, during Sri Lanka’s economic crisis, Australia's Economic Opportunities for the Poor (EOP) investment delivery partners pivoted operations to help leading local firms maintain their supply chains and customer engagement. The ILO’s LEED+ program was adjusted to provide underprivileged communities with decent short-term work and reasonable accommodation to earn wages and continue farming. MDF business partners distributed agricultural supplies to boost farm output and delivered fruit and vegetables to a major supplier, promoting women farmers' backyard gardening to generate revenue and strengthen food security.

title.narrative: Climate adaptation, mitigation, environment and biodiversity

description.narrative:
MDF partnered with a Sri Lankan supermarket chain to improve fresh produce-sourcing during the fertiliser shortage in 2022 which contributed to Sri Lanka's food insecurity crisis. Through the supermarket chain's farmer-network, fertiliser bundles were provided to 200 vegetable farmers (Men 180, Women 20) enabling them to continue production. Over 75% of farmers interviewed by MDF said the fertiliser had increased yield by an average of 56 per cent. MDF calculated that this resulted in an additional USD300,600 (AUD 455, 823) in income for farmers.‍
MDF's partnership with female-run mushroom exporter, Star Mushrooms, provided knowledge and technical support for over 500 farmers (90% women) to expand into controlled environment (protected agriculture) crops and techniques, such as mushroom farming. The intervention succeeded during a period of heavy drought, when farmers faced significant crop losses in open field / conventional farms. The intervention generated almost USD100,000 (AUD 152,000) in additional income for over 220 mushroom-producing households, over 80 per cent of whom were women.

title.narrative: Economic policy reform and management and private sector development

description.narrative: MDF's diversification and expansion processes improve the profitability of the coffee value chain by reducing the time to realise investment returns. The improved profitability of the coffee value chain, resulted in the Sri Lankan government listing coffee as a priority export crop. Key government stakeholders are engaging with MDF to expand the sector. There has also been an increase in independent private investment into the sector, demonstrating the potential for further expansion and sustained growth in the specialty coffee market. Several local cafés which switched to serving locally sourced specialty coffee, when the economic crisis caused restrictions on imported coffee, are continuing to serve local varieties despite restrictions easing

Smallholder tea suppliers are often economically disadvantaged, through inefficient and inequitable purchasing practices in supplier networks. Australia’s Market Development Facility (MDF) program collaborated with Agrithmics, a fintech and automation provider, to implement digital weighing scales at Falcon Tea Factory in Ratnapura, to improve the transparency of the tea weighing process, benefitting over 1,700 smallholder tea suppliers. This initiative aimed to enhance transparency and trust in transactions within the smallholder network. Previously susceptible to income losses from scale tampering during manual weighing, farmers now benefited from tamper-proof digital scales. This intervention led to increased transparency, reduced income loss, and attracted 120 additional farmers to Falcon's network, 76 of whom were women (63%). This enhancement underscores the economic advantages of investing in equitable, farmer-centric supply chain solutions.

The Australian Government funded the ILO's LEED+ program to support 560 women business owners (micro to small scale) and commercial farmers (dry chilli, groundnut, and sea cucumber) in sustainable economic development. The program also helped them gain access to financial, business and market access for the first time. 21 of the women now have a thriving micro to small-scale businesses and gained training in product branding, packaging, safety and health procedures, and business management. 228 women farmers received credit facilities for seeds, fertilizer and machinery services.

The Market Development Facility (MDF) program, funded by Australia and in partnership with Ellawala Horticulture Private Limited, supported the commercial cultivation of mango. The program used new technology to expand an organic backyard farming model and provided farmers with advisory support. The pilot project supported 100 participants harvesting crops and selling surplus produce. The program included educating farmers on the impacts of agrochemical use and changing negative perceptions of subsistence farming. With the expansion of the backyard farming model, farmers were able to sell excess produce, demonstrating the commercial benefits of organic farming. The intervention greatly improved access to safe, nutritious food for communities. Collaboration between MDF and Ellawala Horticulture Pvt Ltd positively impacted local agriculture and sustainable practices.

With Australia's support, the National Apprentice and Industrial Training Authority (NAITA) has implemented the Workforce Development Model which reduced expenses for students and established training centres that collaborate with employers, to implement the training package. By offering work-based training, the total cost for course assessment and certification is kept at an affordable LKR 6,000. In contrast, centre-based training can cost over LKR 50,000. This significant cost difference made training more accessible and affordable for all trainees. ‍ Enterprises and industry institutions are encouraged to become accredited training centres themselves. Several initiatives support this effort, including sharing training materials on tourism-related websites and centres, creating a video guide on the new National Competency Standards (NCS), aligning course materials with these NCS, and providing technical assistance for NAITA media teams. Currently, 42 establishments across four districts can conduct trainings and have undergone training on Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL).

Women contribute significantly to agricultural businesses in Sri Lanka, but they face barriers such as limited market and resource access, low levels of land ownership, and minimal engagement with financial services and technology. They also have disproportionate unpaid care responsibilities, limiting their participation in agriculture. In 2023, the Market Development Facility (a multi-country initiative supported by the Australian Government that promotes sustainable economic development) collaborated with female-run mushroom exporter, Star Mushrooms, to provide business insights and technical expertise. They created a new product-sourcing model that incentivised female-run, home-based businesses through hands-on farmer engagement. Through the model, Star Mushrooms expanded its supplier base from 36 to 220 (80% of whom were women entrepreneurs) and saw revenue growth of 200 per cent within a year. Aiming to grow its network to over one thousand farmers, the new sourcing model has provided Star Mushrooms with the produce volumes required to expand its product range. A firm business case has been developed for Star Mushrooms to support female farmers to reliably access markets.

Women in Sri Lanka face significant barriers to entering and advancing in the tourism sector—particularly in public-facing or non-traditional roles—due to restrictive social norms, safety concerns, and limited access to skills development. Addressing these challenges requires inclusive approaches backed by strong market incentives. Inclusion efforts are most effective when aligned with a clear business case. ‍ With support from the Australian-funded Market Development Facility (MDF), Intrepid is developing a women-led supply base for its new women-only tour offering, designed for solo female travellers and featuring female guides and experience providers. As part of this regional initiative, MDF facilitated collaboration with the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority’s provincial councils to identify and train women interested in tourism roles. ‍ In 2024, 11 women completed training in tour leading, communication, safety and crisis management, cultural sensitivity, and leadership development, with more expected in 2025. Participants came from diverse backgrounds—some already engaged in tourism, others exploring new livelihood opportunities. While not all may join Intrepid’s supply chain, the training equips them to pursue alternative roles in the sector. ‍ This initiative demonstrates how targeted inclusion, driven by market opportunity, can create space for women to thrive in non-traditional economic roles.
